title: Ontario premier calls St. Catharines, Ont., resident to say shelter won't be opening in her neighbourhood | CBC News
text:
When Cathy Link answered her phone Wednesday morning, she said she was stunned to hear  Ontario Premier Doug Ford on the other end.

She was even more surprised when he told her the province was pulling the plug on controversial plans to put an emergency shelter for people experiencing homelessness in her neighbourhood in St. Catharines, Ont.

"I think I even let out a scream," she told CBC News, expressing shock that the premier was calling her directly with what she considered welcome news.

Link is one of the residents living around Bunting and Dunkirk roads, just south of the Garden City Skyway, who have expressed concerns about plans by Niagara's regional government to put a shelter on a vacant site at 154 Bunting Road.

The region needs to open a new shelter in St. Catharines by year's end because its existing lease at a temporary shelter on Riordon Street is set to expire. Regional officials have also emphasized that such facilities are crucial in getting people who are unhoused into safe, stable housing.

But at a city council meeting and a regional committee meeting in July, some residents near the proposed site on Bunting Road argued the shelter would result in vandalism, garbage, and intravenous drug users discarding dirty syringes in Douglas Park, which is kitty-corner to the site.

"People have picnics there, kids play on the playground, and we always have baseball and tournaments there," said Link. "It's always busy.

"I was worried about the kids. They'd lose their safety zone. To me it was a bad choice."

Link had texted Ford to express those fears, using a cell phone number Coun. Jackie Lindal shared with residents to contact the premier with their concerns over the proposed site.

"He's been replying ever since and he's been keeping me updated," she said.

Then on Wednesday morning, she said Ford called her.

"He said they're still looking into it and he's trying to see what he can do," she said. "Ten minutes later he called me [again] and said the lease has been pulled and it's not happening. He said, 'it's done.'"

The region confirmed in a statement to CBC News on Wednesday that lease negotiations for the Bunting Road site have been terminated.

That leaves the region still searching for another site by the end of the year.

"Niagara Region remains committed to securing an appropriate shelter site in St. Catharines and will continue working with the local municipality, community partners, service providers and other levels of government to support a safe, well-managed and housing-focused shelter," housing services director Cameron Banach said in the statement.

City staff have considered 190 potential sites in St. Catharines but none met all the criteria, which include not being too close to schools or too far from public transit, community services commissioner Henri Koning told a regional committee meeting in July.

The region is trying to find a location that meets the needs of clients and the broader community, but this is proving challenging, said Banach.

"Shelter services are essential for supporting people experiencing homelessness or housing instability, including seniors, youth, individuals and families," he said. "They provide a safe place to stay while connecting people with housing, health care and other supports."

Residents raise alarm bells over potential impact of planned shelter in St. Catharines, Ont.

New shelter coming to St. Catharines, Ont., a crucial part of getting people into secure housing: officials

Once a location is confirmed, the region will share information with residents, businesses, service providers and community partners, he said.

Coun. Lindal said she had encouraged residents to contact Ford because she believed the Bunting Road site next to where the skyway will be twinned was one of the worst potential sites for the shelter.

It's far from supports closer to downtown typically accessed by vulnerable people such as a soup kitchen and Start Me Up Niagara, which provides services and programs for people experiencing poverty, homelessness, unemployment and mental health issues, she said.

"I thought it was cruel to put it there," said Lindal. "You're putting it in the middle of a construction zone, you're putting it away from all their supports."

Link, who also said she feared the location would have been bad for users of the shelter, said she was impressed with Ford's willingness to stay in touch with her over a period of weeks and to call directly to inform her the lease talks were dead.

"I thanked him so much," she said. "He was amazing. The whole neighbourhood was together fighting this [but] we thought it was a done deal."

Reporter/editor

Paul Forsyth is a St. Catharines-based CBC reporter covering communities in the Niagara Region. He has decades of reporting experience in Niagara, having worked for Niagara This Week, the St. Catharines Standard and the Welland Tribune before joining CBC. You can reach him at paul.forsyth@cbc.ca.
